clue.text: Marquis's place of origin and deplorable end of life

parts.note: a deplorable state of affairs is a sad one

indicators.note: the end of a word is its last letter

parts.note: the last letter of LIFE

explanation.surface: A biography note on where a notorious aristocrat came from and how miserably he died.
explanation.walkthrough: The Marquis de Sade's title means 'of Sade': Sade is literally the place he came from, so the definition is exact as well as sly.
explanation.definitionFit: The Marquis de Sade took his title from the family's seat, so Sade is where the marquis came from.

clue.text: Toadying special address to queen

definitions.note: Toadying is read as a noun here: 'all that toadying' = 'all that smarm'.

parts.note: S is the standard abbreviation for special
the Queen is addressed as 'ma'am', also spelt MARM

explanation.surface: A courtier fawning in the special speech he makes to the monarch.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface pictures the toadying itself: a special address to the queen is exactly where you would expect smarm.
explanation.definitionFit: Smarm is oily, ingratiating flattery, which is what toadying is.

clue.text: Departs on horseback, editor taken for ride

parts.note: D = departs, as in railway timetables
a jockey who is riding is 'up'
ED is the usual abbreviation for editor

explanation.surface: An editor rides off on a horse, apparently taken for a literal ride.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface makes 'ride' sound like horse-riding, but 'taken for a ride' is the idiom for being tricked. UP for mounted comes from racing: 'Dettori up'.
explanation.definitionFit: To be taken for a ride is to be cheated or fooled, which is to be duped.

clue.text: Bloodsucker — run if heard

indicators.note: the word is to be taken by its sound

parts.note: to run away is to flee, and the spoken word is what counts

explanation.surface: A warning to run for it if you hear a bloodsucker coming.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as a vampire warning, which hides the tiny bloodsucker in plain sight.
explanation.definitionFit: A flea is a parasite that feeds on blood.

clue.text: German chemist's whopping whopper comes first

indicators.note: tells you to put the second item, the whopper, before the first

parts.note: a whopper is a big lie
whopping = very big

explanation.surface: Someone telling an enormous lie at the start of a story about a German scientist.
explanation.walkthrough: Read in order, the clue gives BIG LIE; 'comes first' swaps them. Justus von Liebig was the nineteenth-century chemist behind fertiliser science and the stock cube.
explanation.definitionFit: Justus von Liebig was a leading German chemist of the nineteenth century.

clue.text: Confused case made for scholastic fields

indicators.note: the letters are muddled into a new order

parts.note: anagram fodder, 8 letters

explanation.surface: A lawyer's muddled argument presented to an academic audience.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Case made' reads like a courtroom phrase, pulling away from the university world of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Academe is the world of scholarship; academes are its separate fields or institutions.

clue.text: Dead debauchee Donald Duck?

parts.note: D = dead, as in genealogies
a rake is a dissolute man

explanation.surface: A scandalous suggestion that the cartoon Donald Duck was a dead libertine.
explanation.walkthrough: Donald Duck is a male duck, so he is an example of a drake; the question mark flags that one example standing for the class.
explanation.definitionFit: A drake is a male duck, and Donald is the most famous male duck there is.

clue.text: He makes spirits from infernal world tense, more evil

parts.note: Dis is the Roman god of the underworld, and the underworld itself
T = tense, the grammar abbreviation
ill = evil, so more evil = iller

explanation.surface: A sorcerer summoning spirits from a hellish world that grows tenser and more wicked.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface makes 'spirits' ghosts raised from hell; the answer means whisky and gin.
explanation.definitionFit: A distiller makes spirits such as whisky and gin by distillation.

clue.text: Boy seen in bazaar once

indicators.note: the answer can be seen inside the words that follow

parts.note: bazAAR ONce

explanation.surface: A boy was once spotted at a market.
explanation.walkthrough: A first name defined as 'Boy' is a standard crossword convention.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Aaron, the biblical brother of Moses, is a common boy's first name.

clue.text: Stoicism broken under cane thrashing

indicators.note: something broken is in pieces, ready to be rebuilt
a thrashing knocks things about into disorder

parts.note: anagram fodder, 9 letters

explanation.surface: A pupil's stiff upper lip finally giving way while being caned.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue pictures the answer being tested: stoicism is exactly what a caning demands, so the surface and the definition belong together.
explanation.definitionFit: Stoicism is patient endurance of pain or hardship without complaint.

clue.text: Spaniel regularly seen in boat trip

indicators.note: take letters at a regular interval: here every other one

parts.note: SpAnIeL: the 1st, 3rd, 5th and 7th letters

explanation.surface: A dog that keeps turning up on a boat outing.
explanation.walkthrough: The spaniel on the boat is a pleasant picture that hides a purely letter-level mechanism.
explanation.definitionFit: The noun is named after the canvas that drives the vessel: going for one means an outing on the water.

clue.text: Pacify primate eating some veg

indicators.note: the primate takes the veg inside itself

parts.note: an ape is a primate
peas are a vegetable

explanation.surface: Calming down a monkey by letting it munch vegetables.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is practical advice: feed the ape to keep it quiet, which is itself appeasement.
explanation.definitionFit: To appease someone is to pacify them by giving them what they want.

clue.text: Certain ruses deployed in commercial

indicators.note: the ruses are spread out in a new arrangement
the rearranged letters go inside the advertisement

parts.note: an ad is a commercial
RUSES rearranged

explanation.surface: Advertisers using certain tricks in their commercials.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Certain ruses' reads as 'some tricks', but 'Certain' is the definition meaning sure.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: an outcome that is guaranteed, with no doubt left, is both certain and sure.

clue.text: A girl belonging to me hugs a singer

parts.note: what belongs to me is mine
Adele is the British pop singer

explanation.surface: Someone proudly claiming a girl who embraces a singer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A girl belonging to me' reads as one possessive phrase; it splits after 'girl', and the girl's name is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: this French form of Magdalene is a girl's first name, so 'A girl' stands for it.

clue.text: For audience get weak beer

indicators.note: what an audience gets is the sound of the word

parts.note: to ail is to be sickly and grow weak; only its sound is used

explanation.surface: A sickly, watery beer served to a crowd.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Weak beer' looks like one phrase, but 'weak' belongs to the wordplay and 'beer' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: this top-fermented brew, bitter and pale among them, is one kind of beer.

clue.text: Victor has tip-off in The Bull Ring

definitions.note: The inner is strictly the ring just outside the bull on a target; 'in' links it.

indicators.note: the tip, the first letter, comes off

parts.note: the victor is the winner; its tip, the W, comes off

explanation.surface: A winner getting a racing tip in the Bull Ring, Birmingham's big shopping centre.
explanation.walkthrough: The Bull Ring is a famous Birmingham shopping district, so the capitals point away from darts and archery, where the inner is the ring round the bull's-eye.
explanation.definitionFit: On a target the inner is the ring immediately around the bull, so it is the bull's ring.

clue.text: Hip joints need one piano with singer

parts.note: p = piano, soft in music
Elvis Presley, the singer

explanation.surface: Elvis Presley at the piano, whose swivelling hips were famous.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface earns its keep: Elvis was nicknamed 'Elvis the Pelvis' for his hip movements, so answer and singer are already linked.
explanation.definitionFit: The hip joints are sockets in the pelvis, so each needs one to sit in.

clue.text: Programming language formats rigged for hardware systems

indicators.note: the letters are fixed into a new order

parts.note: PL/I is an old programming language; PL is short for programming language
FORMATS rearranged

explanation.surface: A computing note about a language that fixes file formats for hardware.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole surface stays in computing, so every word looks like part of one technical definition.
explanation.definitionFit: In computing a platform is the hardware and operating system on which software runs.

clue.text: Delay of time for jailbird

definitions.meaning: an interval between cause and effect, as with jet travel
British slang for a convict, usually with 'old' in front

explanation.surface: A prisoner's sentence being put back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old lag' is British slang for a long-serving convict, so a lag is a jailbird.
explanation.definitionFit: A lag is an interval of delay, and in slang a convict.

clue.text: One covers NS&I fraud, standing firm

indicators.note: in a down answer, the item that covers sits above the rest

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral one
NS&I is National Savings and Investments, the British government savings bank; the ampersand drops out
a sting is a confidence trick

explanation.surface: A whistle-blower firmly exposing a fraud at a government savings bank.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Covers' sounds like a cover-up, but in a down clue it just means 'goes on top of'.
explanation.definitionFit: Insisting is holding firm to a demand or claim, standing firm on it.

clue.text: Waterproof clothing waterproofs family

parts.note: to waterproof a joint is to seal it
one's kin is one's family

explanation.surface: A family kitted out in rain gear.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Waterproofs' reads as a plural noun, the family's raincoats; it is a verb meaning seals.
explanation.definitionFit: Sealskin garments are made from seal pelts, naturally water-repellent.

clue.text: Family cat's bitten off lamb's tail

indicators.note: CAT is bitten off the front of the longer word

parts.note: a hazel catkin is popularly called a lamb's tail
remove CAT from CATKIN

explanation.surface: A cat biting the tail off a lamb, to the family's horror.
explanation.walkthrough: The farmyard scene hides a botanical fact: the dangling catkins of hazel are called lambs' tails.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: relatives by blood, one's family, are collectively one's kin.

clue.text: Worked unclean old hotel without a meal

indicators.note: worked means kneaded or reshaped, so the letters are rearranged
without here means lacking, so the letter a is taken out of the pool

parts.note: taken as written, as anagram fodder
Hotel is H in the NATO phonetic alphabet
taken as written: the letter removed

explanation.surface: A grubby old hotel, after some work, still doesn't serve a meal.
explanation.walkthrough: Pool UNCLEAN with O and H, take away the A, and rework what is left; 'Worked' looks like a past tense describing the hotel.
explanation.definitionFit: Luncheon is a formal word for lunch, the midday meal.

clue.text: Imperial leader's gold luxury car touring States (America)

indicators.note: the car travels round the States, containing them

parts.note: Au is the chemical symbol for gold
a GT, gran turismo, is a high-performance touring car
the United States
US = America

explanation.surface: An emperor's gold limousine on a tour of the United States.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Imperial leader's' reads as the possessive; the definition is just the leader, Rome's first emperor.
explanation.definitionFit: Augustus was the first Roman emperor, the leader of the imperial state.

clue.text: Public relations deceptively nice — Charming?

indicators.note: NICE is disguised as a different arrangement

parts.note: PR is public relations
NICE rearranged

explanation.surface: A cynical question about whether a PR man's charm is genuine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Charming' looks like an adjective about the spin doctor; with the question mark it is Prince Charming of the fairy tales.
explanation.definitionFit: Prince Charming is the fairy-tale hero, so a prince is an example of a Charming.

clue.text: Wheel around, turn over

parts.note: c. = circa, around, before a date

indicators.note: the word is turned over, back to front

parts.note: your turn is your go

explanation.surface: An instruction to spin a wheel round and flip it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Around' and 'turn' both look like instructions to the wheel, but they are the letters C and GO.
explanation.definitionFit: Strictly the word names one tooth on a gear, but it is used for the whole toothed wheel.

clue.text: Keeping secret a chastisement

definitions.meaning: concealing something, putting it out of sight
informal British for a thrashing, as in 'a good ...'

explanation.surface: Concealing a punishment.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'hiding' as a thrashing is informal British English: 'give him a good hiding'.
explanation.definitionFit: Hiding means concealing, and a hiding is a physical punishment.

clue.text: Stops eating butter etc around sabbath

indicators.note: to be around something is to surround it

parts.note: butter and the like are fats
S = Sabbath, the abbreviation

explanation.surface: Someone who gives up butter and such for the Sabbath.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is religious abstinence, so 'Stops eating butter' looks like one definition; 'eating' is part of it, and butter is the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: To fast is to go without food, so someone who fasts stops eating.

clue.text: Don, the cycling Norwegian

indicators.note: letters go round from the front to the back, keeping their order

parts.note: Norse = Norwegian; its first three letters go round to the back

explanation.surface: A Norwegian named Don out on his bicycle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Don' looks like a man's name; it is the Spanish title, like Señor.
explanation.definitionFit: Don and señor are both Spanish titles for a gentleman.

clue.text: Caught on shelf one fine fellow's dug in — don't fall off here

indicators.note: the letters are dug into the shelf

parts.note: c = caught, the cricket scorecard abbreviation
a ledge is a shelf
I is the Roman numeral one
F = fine, as on pencils
F = fellow, as in FRS

explanation.surface: A climber caught on a ledge, digging in with a warning not to fall.
explanation.walkthrough: I, F and F go inside LEDGE after its L, with C in front. The definition is a cryptic warning sign rather than a synonym.
explanation.definitionFit: A cliff edge is exactly the place where you must not fall off.

clue.text: Confusion — one of the axes is a stick in the mud

parts.note: to be in a fog is to be confused
the y-axis, alongside x and z

explanation.surface: Muddled talk of which axis is stuck in the mud.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Axes' looks like choppers, which a stick in the mud might suggest; it means graph axes.
explanation.definitionFit: A fogy, usually an old fogy, is someone stuck in old-fashioned ways.

clue.text: Director's squeeze acting in play

parts.note: D = director
to ram things in is to squeeze them in
A = acting, as in an acting officer

explanation.surface: A director's girlfriend given a part in his play.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Squeeze' is British slang for a partner, which makes the casting-couch reading; here it is the verb RAM.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: any work written to be performed by actors, a play, is a drama.

clue.text: Expel college student not much seen

indicators.note: only part of the words shows: the answer is tucked inside

parts.note: collEGE STudent

explanation.surface: A college expelling a student who rarely turns up.
explanation.walkthrough: The truant student is a neat picture for being expelled, and 'not much seen' is the unusual hidden-word signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A technical synonym from biology, the opposite of ingest: discharging waste from the body is expelling it.

clue.text: Program's second minute up — period of execution

indicators.note: second here means the second letter of the word

parts.note: its second letter is R

indicators.note: up in the sense of in disorder, as when a road is up, so the letters are mixed

parts.note: taken as written, as anagram fodder

explanation.surface: A computing note: a program's second minute is over, and its execution period is up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'execution' sounds like a hanging, but in computing a program is executed when it runs; 'second' and 'minute' look like units of time and are neither.
explanation.definitionFit: Run time is the span during which a computer program is executing, or the length of a film.

clue.text: Where fire is laid, no thanks from him

parts.note: where the fire is laid: in ...
a fire is laid in the grate

explanation.surface: An ungrateful guest who won't thank you for laying the fire.
explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay is the phrase 'in grate', the answer to 'where is the fire laid?', run together into one word.
explanation.definitionFit: An ingrate is an ungrateful person, one from whom you get no thanks.

clue.text: Keep mum's carpet — it could go with whatever

parts.note: 'Sh!' tells you to keep mum, to stay quiet
a rug is a small carpet

explanation.surface: Mum's carpet will go with any decor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mum' looks like mother, but 'keep mum' means stay silent. The definition pictures a teenager's shrug alongside a muttered 'whatever'.
explanation.definitionFit: A shrug is the gesture that goes with saying 'whatever', showing indifference.

clue.text: Horses given hitch with head pushed right back

indicators.note: the first letter is moved all the way to the end

parts.note: a hitch is a snag; move its S to the back

explanation.surface: Horses given a harness hitch with their heads pulled back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hitch' suggests hitching horses to a cart; it is a snag, a problem.
explanation.definitionFit: Nags are horses, usually old or poor ones.

clue.text: Transported in parcel paper say?

indicators.note: take the word as it is said aloud

parts.note: something in parcel paper is wrapped; only the sound is used

explanation.surface: Goods sent through the post in brown paper.
explanation.walkthrough: The parcel surface makes 'Transported' mean shipped; it means enraptured.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words describe being carried away by delight or absorption, the figurative sense of 'transported'.
